name: Nimzo-Indian Defense, Zurich Variation
summary: The Zurich Variation answers the Nimzo-Indian's 4.Qc2 with 4...Nc6, developing actively to prepare a piece-supported ...e5 break.
intro: In the Zurich (Milner-Barry) Variation of the Nimzo-Indian, Black meets 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 with the developing 4...Nc6. Rather than striking with the usual ...d5 or ...c5, Black places the knight on c6 to back an eventual ...e5, aiming for piece pressure and rich manoeuvring play.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Qc2 Nc6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: With 4.Qc2 White declines to accept doubled c-pawns, keeping the pawn structure intact and preparing to take the bishop pair with a3. Black's 4...Nc6 is a committal reply: the knight does not block a c-pawn advance here because Black intends ...d6 and ...e5 rather than ...c5, using the centre pawns to open lines for the pieces.

The resulting positions are less about immediate pawn breaks and more about piece coordination and control of the central dark squares. Black's bishop on b4 and knight on c6 generate pressure, and after a timely ...e5 the game can open into sharp middlegames where White's bishop pair competes against Black's active development and central influence.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: White most often continues with a3, questioning the b4-bishop. Black can retreat, or allow the exchange on b4 to double White's own pawns after ...Bxc3+, trading the bishop pair for a firm grip on the dark squares and the e5 outpost. The knight on c6 then supports the central advance and eyes the d4 and e5 squares.

Alternatively White develops naturally with e3, Nf3 or g3 and Bg2, meeting Black's ...d6 and ...e5 plan with central play of his own. Precise move order matters: Black must time ...e5 so that it gains space and freedom rather than conceding the d5 square, while White seeks to exploit the bishop pair and the slightly loose black structure.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation takes its name from the celebrated 1953 Zurich Candidates tournament, one of the greatest events in chess history, where the line received attention at the highest level. It is also associated with Philip Milner-Barry, and the ...Nc6 idea has remained a respected, distinctly strategic answer to the 4.Qc2 Classical Nimzo-Indian ever since.

Trade on c3 when useful to damage White's structure and grip the dark squares
Play for piece activity and central influence over pawn breaks
Contest White's bishop pair with active, coordinated minor pieces
